summary.text: Focal length measures how strongly an optical system converges or diverges light, and for an ideal thin lens it is the distance from the lens to its focal points.
A positive focal length means the system converges light and a negative one means it diverges light, with a shorter focal length bending rays more sharply.
In photography and telescopes, a longer focal length gives higher magnification and a narrower angle of view, while the field of view shrinks as focal length grows.

facts.label: Converging lens
facts.value: Positive focal length, where parallel light is focused to a spot

facts.label: Diverging lens
facts.value: Negative focal length, found by tracing the spread beam backward

items.prompt: You hold a magnifying glass in sunlight and the light gathers into a tiny bright spot on the ground. What is true of the lens's focal length?

options.label: It is negative, because light passes through the glass
It is zero, because the light meets at a point
It is the thickness of the glass at its centre
It is positive, the distance from the lens to the spot

items.explain: For a converging lens the focal length is positive and equals the distance at which a beam of collimated light is focused to a single spot.

items.prompt: A wildlife photographer, standing in the same place, swaps a short camera lens for a much longer one. What changes in the photo?

options.label: The view narrows and the animal looks larger
The view widens and the animal looks smaller
The view stays the same but gets sharper
The view narrows and the animal looks smaller

items.explain: For distant subjects, a longer focal length gives higher magnification and a narrower angle of view.

items.prompt: A microscope maker wants more magnification of a specimen sitting right next to the lens. Which choice moves in the right direction?

options.label: A longer focal length, since it bends light less
A shorter focal length, so the subject can sit closer
A negative focal length, so the image is flipped
A focal length equal to the width of the sensor

items.explain: In close-up work such as microscopy, a shorter focal length gives higher magnification because the subject can be brought closer to the lens.

items.prompt: Two lenses are tested with parallel light. One brings it to a point just 5 cm away, the other only 20 cm away. Which statement is right?

options.label: The 20 cm lens bends rays more sharply
Both bend the rays by exactly the same amount
The 5 cm lens diverges the light while the other converges it
The 5 cm lens bends rays more sharply

items.explain: A shorter focal length bends rays more sharply, bringing them to a focus in a shorter distance.

items.prompt: A laser beam goes through a lens and spreads out. Tracing the spreading rays backward, they appear to meet at one point. What does that point tell you?

options.label: It is the focal point of a diverging lens with a negative focal length
It is where a real image forms on a screen behind the lens
It is the spot where the lens is thickest
It is the point where the laser was focused earlier

items.explain: For a diverging lens, the focal length is negative and is the distance to the point from which a collimated beam appears to diverge; no image forms, so it is found by tracing backward.

items.prompt: A camera with a 50 mm lens is set to focus on a far-away mountain. How far is the sensor behind the lens's rear principal plane?

options.label: Almost nothing, since the mountain is so far
Twice the focal length, to make room for the image
The lens's focal length, so about 50 mm
The distance to the mountain divided by 50

items.explain: With the lens set to infinity, the sensor sits at the focal plane, separated from the rear principal plane by the focal length.

paragraphs.heading: What focal length measures
paragraphs.text: Focal length is a measure of how strongly a lens or other optical system bends light, either drawing rays together or spreading them apart. It is given as a length. For an idealized thin lens, it is simply the distance from the lens to its focal points. A positive value means the system gathers light together, and a negative value means it spreads light out. The shorter the focal length, the more sharply the rays bend, so they meet sooner or fan out faster.

paragraphs.heading: Converging and diverging lenses
paragraphs.text: Picture a collimated beam, meaning a beam of parallel rays, entering a thin lens in air. A converging lens, such as a convex one, brings those rays to a single spot, and the distance to that spot is its focal length. A diverging lens, such as a concave one, sends them outward, and its negative focal length is the distance back to the point the spreading beam seems to come from. A concave lens is somewhat harder to measure. No image forms in the test, so instead you pass a laser beam through it, see how much the beam spreads, and trace it backwards to the focal point.

paragraphs.heading: Optical power
paragraphs.text: For more general optical systems, focal length loses its intuitive picture. It is then just the inverse of the system's optical power, and the quantity 1/f is what optical power means. This value is called the effective focal length, and it is the number used to work out how much the system magnifies. The whole system can then be modelled as one ideal thin lens with the same effective focal length.

paragraphs.heading: Magnification and angle of view
paragraphs.text: Whether a long or short focal length magnifies more depends on how the system is used. In telescopes and most photography the subject is in effect infinitely far away, so a longer focal length gives higher magnification and a narrower angle of view, while a shorter one gives a wider view and less magnification. A microscope works the other way round: the object is brought close to the lens, and a shorter focal length magnifies more because the subject can sit closer. In general, focal length and field of view are inversely proportional.

paragraphs.heading: Focal length in a camera
paragraphs.text: Camera lens focal lengths are usually stated in millimetres, though some older lenses are marked in centimetres or inches. Focal length is measured from a reference plane in the lens called the rear principal plane. When a camera lens is set to infinity, that plane sits one focal length away from the film or sensor, so distant objects form sharp images there. Take a normal 50 mm lens on a 35 mm camera: to focus something far away, its rear principal plane must be 50 mm from the film plane. As the object comes closer, that lens-to-film distance has to grow.

paragraphs.heading: Front, rear and the human eye
paragraphs.text: In air or a vacuum, the front, rear and effective focal lengths are all the same, so you can just say focal length. In any other medium, the front and rear focal lengths equal the effective focal length multiplied by the refractive index of whatever medium lies before or behind the lens. The plain phrase focal length then becomes ambiguous. This difference matters for the human eye, which can be modelled either as a thin lens at a boundary between air and fluid, or as a different thin lens sitting entirely in air with the eye's effective focal length.
